title: Praxis Special Education: Teaching Students with Behavioral Disorders and Emotional Disturbances (5372) - 200 Source Questions + 300 Guided Review
description: Contains 200 original source questions, 0 assistant-authored independent practice questions, and 300 source-derived guided-review activities. The assistant audit found 115 distinct independent content kernels. Two 100-item diagnostics, an exact-blueprint 120-item simulation, detailed feedback, and native learning support for K-12 EBD specialists.
contentReview: Assistant audit completed: 200 independent-practice items contain 115 distinct content kernels and 85 parallel variants under the normalized test. 300 additional activities are guided reasoning transformations, not independent exam questions. The 500-distinct-question target is not met.
simulationLabel: 120-question Behavioral Disorders and Emotional Disturbances simulation
disclaimer: Independent preparation material, not affiliated with or endorsed by ETS. Results are not official forms, scaled scores, pass predictions, licenses, diagnoses, eligibility, placement, FBA or BIP determinations, mental-health or crisis services, medical or legal advice, or substitutes for individualized assessment and current requirements.

domains.label: Development and Characteristics of Students with EBD
Planning and Managing the Learning Environments

items.prompt: When interpreting behavioral or emotional development, a kindergarten teacher notices that one child reaches several language milestones later than classmates. What is the most appropriate first interpretation?
choices: Broad developmental patterns allow wide variation, so the team should gather multi-source evidence across settings before drawing conclusions.
Falling below the typical classroom average on language milestones establishes a developmental disability that warrants formal eligibility.
The team should assign a provisional disability label promptly so specialized speech-language interventions can begin before gathering family input.
Chronological age norms become uninformative once a child trails classmates, so expectations should be based on informal adult impressions instead.
items.rationale: Milestones provide useful reference points, not stand-alone diagnoses. Educators should document functioning across domains, contexts, and time and involve qualified team members before attributing a pattern to disability. For 5372 preparation, define behavior observably, examine ecological and instructional context, distinguish correlation from function, teach a usable replacement skill, use the least intensive effective response, preserve dignity and belonging, and monitor both outcomes and implementation.

Classroom averages reflect one peer group rather than a diagnostic standard, and early language variation can stem from experience, exposure, or home-language patterns rather than a disability.
Assigning a provisional disability label before multidisciplinary evaluation and family input bypasses IDEA safeguards and risks misidentifying typical developmental variation as an impairment.
Chronological age remains an essential benchmark for interpreting developmental expectations and selecting age-respectful instructional routines, even when a learner needs targeted supports.

items.prompt: When interpreting behavioral or emotional development, a student solves multistep problems during small-group instruction but rarely begins the same work during a noisy whole-class period. What should the teacher examine first?
choices: Conclude that the student has not yet retained the underlying academic skill and re-teach the lesson from the beginning.
Compare task demands, environmental conditions, supports, and performance across both settings.
Lower the academic complexity of the independent assignment so the student can finish without using classroom supports.
Treat the drop in task initiation during the busier period as willful avoidance and add a stricter compliance consequence.
items.rationale: Performance reflects an interaction among learner skills, task demands, supports, and context. Comparing conditions can identify a removable barrier before the team changes expectations or infers a stable trait. For 5372 preparation, define behavior observably, examine ecological and instructional context, distinguish correlation from function, teach a usable replacement skill, use the least intensive effective response, preserve dignity and belonging, and monitor both outcomes and implementation.
choiceRationales: Because the student already demonstrates the skill in the structured setting, the gap points to contextual or support barriers rather than a loss of conceptual understanding.

Correct. Performance reflects an interaction among learner skills, task demands, supports, and context. Comparing conditions can identify a removable barrier before the team changes expectations or infers a stable trait. For 5372 preparation, define behavior observably, examine ecological and instructional context, distinguish correlation from function, teach a usable replacement skill, use the least intensive effective response, preserve dignity and belonging, and monitor both outcomes and implementation.

items.prompt: When interpreting behavioral or emotional development, a multilingual learner has difficulty following rapid oral directions in English but demonstrates the task after a peer models it. Which interpretation is best?
choices: Difficulty demonstrating understanding through rapid English oral tasks provides sufficient evidence to suspect an intellectual disability.
Peer modeling and visual representations should be removed during checks so the teacher can measure the student’s true academic mastery.
Information about how the student performs in the home language is outside school accountability and should be set aside during planning.

items.prompt: When interpreting behavioral or emotional development, a middle school student receiving behavioral or emotional support is embarrassed when an adult uses age-inappropriate materials for a functional routine. What principle should guide revision?

Assign helpful classmates to perform the functional routine for the student so embarrassing instructional materials are unnecessary.

items.prompt: When interpreting behavioral or emotional development, a student performs a social routine only with one familiar adult. Which plan best promotes generalization?
choices: Continue drilling the skill in the original instructional setting until accuracy stays high across several additional months.
Teach across planned variations in people, materials, and natural settings, then fade prompts.
Introduce multiple unrelated social and communication targets simultaneously so the student practices broader flexibility right away.
End direct instruction once mastery appears in the familiar setting and monitor whether transfer emerges spontaneously over time.

Correct. Generalization is more likely when instruction deliberately varies relevant people, materials, and settings, reinforces the skill in natural routines, and gradually transfers stimulus control away from adult prompts. items.prompt: When interpreting behavioral or emotional development, a team is writing a learner profile. Which statement is most useful for planning?
choices: The student performs at a low-functioning developmental level across most structured and unstructured school routines.
Because the student has an autism diagnosis, the student prefers fixed classroom schedules and dislikes unexpected changes.
The student completes a two-step visual routine independently and needs one verbal cue when steps change.

choiceRationales: Broad deficit labels such as low-functioning are non-specific, lack measurable baseline data, and fail to show what the student can already do or which prompts help.

items.prompt: When interpreting behavioral or emotional development, a learner’s participation drops after a recent family move and change in transportation. How should the school respond?
choices: Attribute the sudden drop in classroom participation to progression of the student’s underlying disability profile.
Recommend moving the student to a more restrictive special education classroom so academic expectations can be reduced.
Keep classroom planning focused on curriculum pacing because housing and transportation factors fall outside school instruction.
Weigh environmental disruptions alongside disability needs and coordinate supports respectfully.

choiceRationales: Blaming an acute performance drop on an existing disability overlooks clear situational stressors such as disrupted sleep, attendance, or routines that require stabilization supports.

Revise the instructional program right away because the most recent classroom observation reflects the student’s current true level.

Postpone gathering additional evidence until the scheduled annual IEP meeting so classroom routines remain uninterrupted.
items.rationale: A single observation may be affected by health, context, fatigue, or task features. items.prompt: For a student with behavioral or emotional support needs, a student with autism covers their ears during fire-drill announcements and then misses directions. Which support is most responsive?

items.prompt: For a student with behavioral or emotional support needs, which information is essential when considering educational needs associated with intellectual disability?
choices: A standardized oral reading fluency and comprehension score collected during a single school screening window.
Combined data on cognitive functioning and adaptive behavior across conceptual, social, and practical domains.
Medical history records and physical growth measurements gathered from the student’s primary health-care provider.
Anecdotal teacher ratings describing the student’s adherence to rules inside one general education classroom.

Educational planning therefore considers functional conceptual, social, and practical performance across relevant environments. For 5372 preparation, define behavior observably, examine ecological and instructional context, distinguish correlation from function, teach a usable replacement skill, use the least intensive effective response, preserve dignity and belonging, and monitor both outcomes and implementation.
choiceRationales: A single academic reading measure cannot capture broader intellectual functioning or everyday social and practical adaptive skills needed to plan comprehensive supports.

Correct. Intellectual disability involves limitations in intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior. items.prompt: When an access, regulation, sensory, or health factor may affect behavior, a student who is deaf uses sign language and will join a fast-paced seminar. Which plan best supports equitable access?

Assign front-row seating near the teacher’s desk as the primary accommodation for full seminar participation.
Replace live seminar discussions with written summaries so the student can earn participation credit independently.
Maintain rapid open-floor discussions without turn-taking cues so the student experiences realistic peer pacing.
items.rationale: Communication access is broader than hearing volume. Planning should address the learner’s language and mode, visibility or audibility of speakers, technology, peer access, and direct instruction needs. For 5372 preparation, define behavior observably, examine ecological and instructional context, distinguish correlation from function, teach a usable replacement skill, use the least intensive effective response, preserve dignity and belonging, and monitor both outcomes and implementation.
choiceRationales: Correct. Communication access is broader than hearing volume. Planning should address the learner’s language and mode, visibility or audibility of speakers, technology, peer access, and direct instruction needs. For 5372 preparation, define behavior observably, examine ecological and instructional context, distinguish correlation from function, teach a usable replacement skill, use the least intensive effective response, preserve dignity and belonging, and monitor both outcomes and implementation.
Front-row seating alone cannot provide access to rapid multi-speaker peer dialogue, sign-language interpretation, visual turn-taking, or assistive listening needs.
Replacing live peer discussion with solitary written work restricts inclusive interaction and denies authentic communication participation with classmates.
Unstructured overlapping speech makes speechreading, interpreting, and assistive listening far less effective; clear speaker identification supports equitable access.

items.prompt: When an access, regulation, sensory, or health factor may affect behavior, a student with a physical disability needs help reaching and steadying materials during science lab. What is the teacher’s best action?
choices: Assign the student to record observations from the side of the room during laboratory investigations for safety.
Collaborate with the student and specialists to arrange safe positioning and active lab participation.
Adjust the student’s wheelchair seating and lab reach setup independently based on quick classroom judgment.
Ask a lab partner to make experimental decisions and manipulate every tool while the student watches the steps.
items.rationale: Physical access should enable meaningful participation and follow established safety, positioning, and equipment guidance. Collaboration prevents unsafe improvisation and avoids unnecessary removal of learner agency. For 5372 preparation, define behavior observably, examine ecological and instructional context, distinguish correlation from function, teach a usable replacement skill, use the least intensive effective response, preserve dignity and belonging, and monitor both outcomes and implementation.
choiceRationales: Relegating the student to a passive observer role restricts hands-on science participation when adapted equipment or accessible lab stations can support direct involvement.

Correct. Physical access should enable meaningful participation and follow established safety, positioning, and equipment guidance. Collaboration prevents unsafe improvisation and avoids unnecessary removal of learner agency. For 5372 preparation, define behavior observably, examine ecological and instructional context, distinguish correlation from function, teach a usable replacement skill, use the least intensive effective response, preserve dignity and belonging, and monitor both outcomes and implementation.
Improvising physical positioning without OT/PT or student guidance risks discomfort, injury, or equipment instability and bypasses the established health and safety plan.
Having a peer take over experimental decisions strips away cognitive agency; even when a partner assists physically, the student can direct steps and control adapted tools.

items.prompt: When an access, regulation, sensory, or health factor may affect behavior, a student has a documented seizure action plan. During a classroom seizure, what should staff do first?
choices: Improvise a quick classroom response based on staff intuition rather than pausing to follow written health protocols.
Offer water, a small snack, or an unprescribed comfort remedy to help stabilize the student during the episode.
Follow the individualized emergency protocol, protect safety, and activate trained medical procedures.
Wait to initiate school emergency procedures until a parent or guardian can be reached by telephone for guidance.
items.rationale: Health supports in school must follow the individualized plan, staff training, delegation rules, and emergency procedures. Improvised treatment can create risk and exceed an educator’s role. For 5372 preparation, define behavior observably, examine ecological and instructional context, distinguish correlation from function, teach a usable replacement skill, use the least intensive effective response, preserve dignity and belonging, and monitor both outcomes and implementation.
choiceRationales: Improvising outside the individualized health plan increases medical risk and violates school nursing delegation and emergency-response protocols.
Giving unauthorized food, liquid, or medication during a seizure or acute health event can cause choking or dangerous medical complications.

Correct. Health supports in school must follow the individualized plan, staff training, delegation rules, and emergency procedures. Improvised treatment can create risk and exceed an educator’s role. For 5372 preparation, define behavior observably, examine ecological and instructional context, distinguish correlation from function, teach a usable replacement skill, use the least intensive effective response, preserve dignity and belonging, and monitor both outcomes and implementation.
Delaying emergency action until family contact is made wastes critical response time; staff must follow the written medical plan first and notify families per protocol.

items.prompt: When an access, regulation, sensory, or health factor may affect behavior, which goal best addresses adaptive behavior?
choices: Over the upcoming grading period, the student will demonstrate noticeably greater daily independence across school routines.
By the end of the annual review cycle, the student will achieve higher composite scores on a standardized intelligence test.
During school hours, the student will perform everyday self-care and social routines identically to same-age classmates.
Given a visual checklist, the student will complete four cafeteria-purchasing steps in four of five trials.
items.rationale: Adaptive goals should identify a meaningful conceptual, social, or practical routine and specify observable conditions, performance, and criteria. Vague comparisons do not support instruction or progress monitoring. For 5372 preparation, define behavior observably, examine ecological and instructional context, distinguish correlation from function, teach a usable replacement skill, use the least intensive effective response, preserve dignity and belonging, and monitor both outcomes and implementation.
choiceRationales: Broad phrases such as noticeably greater independence lack observable behaviors, conditions, and mastery criteria, making objective progress monitoring impossible.
Standardized intelligence scores measure broad cognitive constructs rather than functional adaptive routines and are not appropriate targets for annual IEP goals.
Requiring identical performance to peers ignores individualized accommodations and fails to define specific, measurable functional steps the team can teach and track.

Correct. Adaptive goals should identify a meaningful conceptual, social, or practical routine and specify observable conditions, performance, and criteria. Vague comparisons do not support instruction or progress monitoring. For 5372 preparation, define behavior observably, examine ecological and instructional context, distinguish correlation from function, teach a usable replacement skill, use the least intensive effective response, preserve dignity and belonging, and monitor both outcomes and implementation.

items.prompt: During multistep algebra, a student begins arguing only after repeated errors on the prerequisite fraction step. What should the special educator do first?
choices: Assess the prerequisite fraction skill, explicitly model it, guide practice, and track accuracy and engagement.
Escalate disciplinary consequences for arguing in class before modifying any prerequisite mathematics instruction.
Remove grade-level algebra instruction from the student’s schedule until behavioral incidents stop across all periods.
Grant open-ended hallway breaks after every algebra mistake without teaching or scaffolding the fraction prerequisite.
items.rationale: The task-specific pattern points to an instructional mismatch that should be assessed directly. Teaching the prerequisite while preserving access to the larger learning goal addresses the likely barrier and produces data on academic and behavioral change.
choiceRationales: Correct. The task-specific pattern points to an instructional mismatch that should be assessed directly. Teaching the prerequisite while preserving access to the larger learning goal addresses the likely barrier and produces data on academic and behavioral change.
Punishing arguing before addressing a clear prerequisite skill bottleneck ignores the documented academic trigger and often escalates avoidance during math.
Removing grade-level algebra restricts curriculum access unnecessarily when the student already solves equations accurately once fraction barriers are addressed.
Providing unguided breaks after errors reinforces task escape while leaving the missing fraction skill untaught and unresolved.

items.prompt: A student disengages during long reading assignments but participates when the same text is divided into short, purposeful segments. Which support best preserves the learning goal?
choices: Replace the assigned grade-level text with brief, unrelated recall worksheets that require minimal reading effort.
Chunk the text, preview its purpose, offer a bounded response choice, teach a help request, and monitor comprehension.
Require quiet, uninterrupted completion of the entire reading passage before offering check-ins or instructional supports.
Award behavior points for seated silence during reading blocks without collecting data on content comprehension.
items.rationale: Chunking and a taught request reduce a predictable response-effort barrier without lowering the content target. Monitoring comprehension and engagement shows whether the preventive and instructional supports improve meaningful access.
choiceRationales: Substituting unrelated easy worksheets lowers academic expectations and denies content-area learning when chunking preserves the original rigorous text.

Correct. Chunking and a taught request reduce a predictable response-effort barrier without lowering the content target. Monitoring comprehension and engagement shows whether the preventive and instructional supports improve meaningful access.
Withholding scaffolds until an overwhelming passage is finished intensifies the exact response-effort trigger that drives off-task behavior.
Rewarding quiet posture without checking comprehension mistakes passive compliance for actual reading understanding and educational progress.

items.prompt: Publicly pointing out errors reliably precedes a student shouting and leaving the group. Which feedback practice is most appropriate during instruction?
choices: Continue announcing academic errors aloud during group lessons so the student builds resilience to peer feedback.
Discontinue correcting the student’s academic mistakes for the semester to avoid triggering classroom escalation.
Deliver brief, neutral, private correction followed by a supported opportunity to respond accurately.
Remove the student from the classroom to the hallway after every incorrect response that causes frustration.
items.rationale: Private, neutral feedback changes a documented antecedent while retaining instruction. An immediate successful response builds the academic skill and lets the teacher reinforce persistence rather than inadvertently strengthening escape or public conflict.
choiceRationales: Persisting with a known public-embarrassment trigger escalates conflict and undermines trust when private feedback delivers the same instructional correction safely.
Stopping all error correction sacrifices academic growth and prevents the student from learning accurate content or receiving supportive feedback.

Correct. Private, neutral feedback changes a documented antecedent while retaining instruction. An immediate successful response builds the academic skill and lets the teacher reinforce persistence rather than inadvertently strengthening escape or public conflict.
Removing the student after mistakes inadvertently reinforces escape from challenging work while reducing instructional time and peer belonging.

items.prompt: A student tears up an independent writing task when asked to organize several ideas but completes one-sentence responses accurately. What is the strongest initial instructional plan?
choices: Assign longer multi-paragraph writing prompts without scaffolds to test whether refusal reflects low effort.
Have a paraprofessional compose and write every extended paragraph response so frustration does not recur.
Interpret all worksheet tearing as peer attention seeking without comparing brief and multi-paragraph writing demands.
Assess paragraph planning, model one clear step with a visual organizer, and reinforce starting and asking for help.
items.rationale: The uneven performance identifies a specific component for assessment and explicit instruction. A scaffolded first step plus an efficient help response preserves writing access, reduces escape value, and supports gradual independence.
choiceRationales: Increasing unassisted writing volume amplifies the exact organizational barrier driving task tearing and provides no explicit strategy instruction.
Having an adult write every response removes student authorship, builds prompt dependence, and substitutes completion for teaching planning skills.
Assuming an attention function without analyzing the contrast between brief and extended writing tasks leads to a mismatched intervention.

Correct. The uneven performance identifies a specific component for assessment and explicit instruction. A scaffolded first step plus an efficient help response preserves writing access, reduces escape value, and supports gradual independence.

items.prompt: A learner often becomes frustrated after teachers give several directions at once and then misses steps. Which instructional adjustment is most likely to help?
choices: Provide concise single-step directions with a visual checklist, verify understanding, and fade support gradually.
Repeat the complete multi-step verbal direction more loudly each time the student misses an expected step.
Exclude the student from laboratory activities and multistep classroom routines to avoid direction overload.
Wait until frustration escalates after missed steps and assign a classroom penalty for failing to follow directions.
items.rationale: Reducing language load and making the sequence visible addresses the documented antecedent while teaching task completion. Checking understanding and fading the checklist prevent the support from becoming a permanent adult prompt.
choiceRationales: Correct. Reducing language load and making the sequence visible addresses the documented antecedent while teaching task completion. Checking understanding and fading the checklist prevent the support from becoming a permanent adult prompt.
Repeating lengthy oral instructions louder does not lower working-memory load and can intensify sensory stress and power struggles.
Excluding the student from multistep labs restricts curriculum access when concise visual checklists can support safe, independent participation.
Penalizing missed steps after cognitive overload punishes an instructional delivery barrier instead of modifying how directions are presented.

items.prompt: High error rates during new vocabulary practice are followed by avoidance. Which lesson design best combines prevention and explicit instruction?
choices: Present unbroken blocks of unfamiliar vocabulary terms until the student stops withdrawing from hard practice.
Intermix known and new items, model responses explicitly, guide frequent practice, and adjust pacing from data.
Transition the student to preferred free-choice time whenever an initial mistake appears on new material.
Reinforce quiet seated posture during vocabulary lessons while disregarding whether target words are mastered.
items.rationale: Interspersal and guided responding create achievable success while the new skill is taught systematically. Joint academic and engagement data show whether pacing and support are reducing errors rather than simply suppressing visible behavior.
choiceRationales: Unbroken blocks of difficult practice keep error rates high, increasing frustration and strengthening escape-maintained withdrawal from classroom instruction.

Correct. Interspersal and guided responding create achievable success while the new skill is taught systematically. Joint academic and engagement data show whether pacing and support are reducing errors rather than simply suppressing visible behavior.
Granting free time right after an error reinforces task escape and interrupts the guided practice needed to master new vocabulary.
Reinforcing quiet classroom compliance without tracking vocabulary accuracy conceals persistent learning gaps behind superficial behavioral stillness.

items.prompt: A student completes assignments in a quiet conference but not in a busy cooperative group. What should the team conclude?
choices: Conclude that the student is deliberately refusing to collaborate because the underlying academic skill is present.
Move all of the student’s core instruction into an isolated one-to-one setting for the remainder of the semester.
Compare task demands, noise, peer interaction, cues, and reinforcement across settings, then test a targeted support.
Apply a standard schoolwide behavior package assigned to every student who shares the same support profile.
items.rationale: A setting difference is evidence to investigate, not proof of motive. Comparing ecological and instructional variables supports a testable, least-intensive adjustment and avoids unnecessary segregation or label-based assumptions.
choiceRationales: Inferring deliberate refusal overlooks real sensory, social, and cueing differences between quiet conferences and busy cooperative groups.
Shifting permanently to an isolated setting violates LRE principles before testing whether modest environmental or role supports enable group success.

Correct. A setting difference is evidence to investigate, not proof of motive. Comparing ecological and instructional variables supports a testable, least-intensive adjustment and avoids unnecessary segregation or label-based assumptions.
Applying a generic label-based package ignores the specific ecological contrast that points directly to testable classroom adjustments.

items.prompt: Assessment shows that missing multiplication facts make grade-level problem solving slow and aversive. Which response maintains ambitious instruction?
choices: Postpone all grade-level problem-solving lessons until every multiplication fact is memorized automatically.
Supply finished computational answers on every assignment so prerequisite fact instruction is no longer needed.
Target classroom behavior management first and assume prerequisite math facts will catch up indirectly.
Teach the prerequisite explicitly while maintaining supported grade-level problem solving and tracking both.
items.rationale: Concurrent instruction avoids an all-or-nothing choice between remediation and meaningful curriculum access. Data on the prerequisite and grade-level application reveal whether support is improving competence and reducing the task barrier.
choiceRationales: Withholding grade-level math until full fact memorization denies ambitious conceptual instruction and often increases stigma and disengagement.
Giving away answers without teaching the prerequisite leaves the underlying fluency bottleneck unresolved and creates lasting dependence.
Focusing solely on behavior without addressing the aversive academic skill barrier fails to remove the root trigger of task frustration.

Correct. Concurrent instruction avoids an all-or-nothing choice between remediation and meaningful curriculum access. Data on the prerequisite and grade-level application reveal whether support is improving competence and reducing the task barrier.

items.prompt: A plan rewards assignment completion, but accuracy remains low and the student never uses the taught help request. Which data are needed to judge the plan?
choices: Track academic accuracy, independent engagement, replacement-skill use, and implementation fidelity together.
Count total completed worksheet pages each afternoon because completion volume captures instructional success.
Raise tangible reward frequency whenever accuracy slips so motivation to finish assignments remains high.
Evaluate plan effectiveness at the end of the grading term using informal recollections from classroom staff.
items.rationale: Completion alone can conceal errors, prompt dependence, or absence of the replacement skill. Multiple direct measures and fidelity evidence distinguish genuine instructional benefit from superficial compliance.
choiceRationales: Correct. Completion alone can conceal errors, prompt dependence, or absence of the replacement skill. Multiple direct measures and fidelity evidence distinguish genuine instructional benefit from superficial compliance.
Page-completion counts can hide rapid guessing, low conceptual accuracy, heavy adult prompting, and zero use of the replacement communication skill.
Increasing rewards for inaccurate work reinforces rushing rather than learning and fails to diagnose why accuracy and help-seeking remain low.
Informal end-of-term impressions lack direct baseline, accuracy, replacement-behavior, and fidelity evidence needed for timely instructional changes.

items.prompt: A multilingual student pauses before responding and becomes quiet during unfamiliar language-heavy tasks. What should guide interpretation of the behavior?
choices: Classify extended pausing and classroom silence as task defiance and initiate a formal consequence ladder.
Examine language access, task load, cultural context, and performance across people and settings with varied evidence.
Treat withdrawal during one English-only observation as sufficient evidence to suspect an emotional disorder.
Set family background and home-language input aside so classroom behavior is scored identically for all peers.
items.rationale: Culturally and linguistically responsive assessment separates an access mismatch from a behavioral hypothesis. Multiple contexts and informants reduce bias and help the team choose instruction based on observable need rather than assumption.
choiceRationales: Treating second-language processing time as willful defiance misreads a linguistic access barrier and risks inequitable disciplinary escalation.

Correct. Culturally and linguistically responsive assessment separates an access mismatch from a behavioral hypothesis. Multiple contexts and informants reduce bias and help the team choose instruction based on observable need rather than assumption.
Drawing an emotional-disorder hypothesis from one English-heavy observation ignores strong participation in accessible contexts and violates multi-source safeguards.
Omitting family cultural background and home-language context obscures critical explanatory evidence and undermines culturally responsive, unbiased behavioral assessment.

items.prompt: A student escapes difficult assignments by yelling and already responds to a visual cue. Which replacement communication should be taught first?
choices: Teach the student to deliver a verbal apology after leaving the classroom and returning from the hallway.
Require the student to write a detailed multi-sentence explanation before any instructional help is offered.
Teach a brief, accessible help or break request that earns a prompt response and a planned return to work.
Allow open-ended dismissal from every difficult assignment whenever frustration signals first appear.
items.rationale: A functionally equivalent request must be easier and more efficient than the problem behavior while still preserving instruction. Prompt reinforcement followed by a supported return makes the replacement usable and sustainable.
choiceRationales: An after-the-fact apology does not replace the escape function during task overload or prevent yelling and leaving the instructional area.
Requiring a lengthy written explanation during high distress makes the replacement far more effortful than yelling, so the student will not use it.

Correct. A functionally equivalent request must be easier and more efficient than the problem behavior while still preserving instruction. Prompt reinforcement followed by a supported return makes the replacement usable and sustainable.
Permitting permanent escape from challenging tasks reinforces avoidance and halts academic growth instead of pairing brief relief with a supported return.

items.prompt: A student uses insults when trying to enter a peer activity. Which communication lesson best matches the likely social function?
choices: Assign enjoyable solitary recreation routines so the student avoids the stress of approaching peer groups.
Deliver a thorough public verbal lecture explaining social rules after every unsuccessful peer interaction.
Award behavior points for remaining completely silent beside peer games without teaching how to join in.
Model and rehearse a concise peer-entry phrase with feedback, then coach supported practice in natural games.
items.rationale: Direct teaching and natural rehearsal address the social outcome the student is seeking. Feedback and supported peer opportunities build a response that can contact the same reinforcement as the challenging behavior.
choiceRationales: Routing the student into solitary play removes opportunities to practice social inclusion and fails to satisfy the student’s desire to join peers.
Public lecturing after peer friction increases embarrassment and resentment without providing coached rehearsal of a workable entry phrase.
Rewarding passive silence does not teach a socially effective way to enter games, leaving the underlying skill gap unresolved.

Correct. Direct teaching and natural rehearsal address the social outcome the student is seeking. Feedback and supported peer opportunities build a response that can contact the same reinforcement as the challenging behavior.

items.prompt: A writing prompt asks students to describe a frightening personal event, and a learner shows distress. Which adjustment preserves access and privacy?
choices: Offer private, non-disclosing topic and response-mode options that still measure the target writing skill.
Require personal disclosure on the original topic because reflective prompts are part of the written syllabus.
Excuse the student from participating in upcoming writing units to avoid potential emotional discomfort.
Invite supportive classmates to share their own stories first so the student feels encouraged to disclose.
items.rationale: The writing construct can be assessed without compelled personal disclosure. Meaningful choices protect dignity and emotional safety while maintaining the academic goal and participation.
choiceRationales: Correct. The writing construct can be assessed without compelled personal disclosure. Meaningful choices protect dignity and emotional safety while maintaining the academic goal and participation.
Compelling students to write about frightening personal experiences compromises emotional safety and privacy when other topics assess the exact same writing construct.
Excusing the student from writing instruction lowers academic access unnecessarily when non-disclosing topic choices preserve full participation.
Peer pressure to disclose sensitive personal experiences violates learner privacy and trauma-aware boundaries rather than offering safe academic choice.

items.prompt: A student uses AAC to request space during early escalation, but staff remove the device to prevent damage. What should the team plan?
choices: Store all communication devices out of reach whenever early signs of emotional distress appear in class.
Keep communication accessible, arrange safe mounting or backup with AAC specialists, and honor requests.
Require spoken verbal requests before honoring a break or space request during heightened emotion.
Allow individual classroom adults to decide informally whether a student’s AAC request is valid that day.
items.rationale: Removing communication access can eliminate the very replacement response intended to prevent escalation. Safe positioning, partner consistency, and prompt reinforcement support autonomy and make the plan functionally coherent.
choiceRationales: Removing AAC during early dysregulation eliminates the learner’s safe replacement voice and reliably drives more intense behavioral escalation.

Correct. Removing communication access can eliminate the very replacement response intended to prevent escalation. Safe positioning, partner consistency, and prompt reinforcement support autonomy and make the plan functionally coherent.
Demanding spoken speech from an AAC user during stress removes functional communication access at the exact moment it is needed most.
Inconsistent adult responses make the AAC request unreliable, undermining trust and causing the student to revert to faster problem behaviors.

items.prompt: A learner wants to request a quieter testing location without relying on an adult to speak first. What is the best instructional approach?
choices: Have a special educator or aide submit the testing-location request on the student’s behalf indefinitely.
Encourage the student to demand any preferred room during tests without referencing the written IEP plan.
Teach when and how to request the accommodation, rehearse across partners, honor requests, and track independence.
Wait until the student earns a failing quiz score in the noisy room before reviewing the accommodation.
items.rationale: Self-advocacy requires explicit knowledge, a practicable communication form, and opportunities to generalize. Measuring independent requests shows whether prompts can be faded while the documented accommodation remains accessible.
choiceRationales: Having adults request accommodations permanently fosters dependence and deprives the student of self-advocacy skills needed across classes and adulthood.
Demanding unaligned classroom settings without linking requests to documented IEP accommodations undermines realistic, constructive student self-advocacy skills.

Correct. Self-advocacy requires explicit knowledge, a practicable communication form, and opportunities to generalize. Measuring independent requests shows whether prompts can be faded while the documented accommodation remains accessible.
Waiting for academic failure before addressing accommodation use causes avoidable harm and delays teaching proactive self-advocacy.

items.prompt: A new help-request skill is taught, but staff respond several minutes later while problem behavior produces an immediate break. What change is most important?
choices: Expand the coping-card routine into several written reflection steps so it feels more academically rigorous.
Withhold adult responses to both the coping card and yelling until the student sits quietly for ten minutes.
Eliminate challenging academic assignments whenever the student enters the classroom to prevent requests.
Make the replacement efficient, honor it promptly and consistently, and teach a clear return routine.
items.rationale: A replacement is unlikely to compete when it is slower or less reliable than the behavior it replaces. Timely, consistent responses establish its value, and the return routine protects continued instructional access.
choiceRationales: Adding extra steps increases response effort and makes the coping card even less competitive against rapid yelling.
Ignoring the taught replacement request extinguishes the very skill staff want to build and risks severe extinction bursts or escalation.
Removing all challenging academic instruction avoids teaching practical coping and self-advocacy skills while sacrificing meaningful educational progress.

Correct. A replacement is unlikely to compete when it is slower or less reliable than the behavior it replaces. Timely, consistent responses establish its value, and the return routine protects continued instructional access.

items.prompt: A student uses a constructive disagreement phrase with one counselor but not with teachers or family. Which plan best promotes generalization?
choices: Align common cues and partner responses across natural settings while tracking student use and adult fidelity.
Continue rehearsing the phrase with the same counselor in the original office until delivery is effortless.
Conclude that classroom transfer is complete once office accuracy is high and end progress monitoring.
Ask each teacher and parent to improvise a distinct classroom response so the student practices flexibility.
items.rationale: Generalization is programmed through varied examples, common essential cues, and consistent consequences. Student and fidelity data help the team identify whether transfer failure reflects instruction or inconsistent partner response.
choiceRationales: Correct. Generalization is programmed through varied examples, common essential cues, and consistent consequences. Student and fidelity data help the team identify whether transfer failure reflects instruction or inconsistent partner response.
Continuing isolated drills in one office strengthens narrow setting-specific stimulus control instead of transferring the phrase to real classes and home.
Discontinuing data collection before verifying natural-setting use leaves generalization unmeasured and risks losing the newly taught skill.
Uncoordinated partner responses confuse the learner about whether the constructive phrase actually works across classrooms and adults.

items.prompt: After a conflict, staff want a student to make a public apology immediately while still visibly distressed. What is a more educationally useful approach?
choices: Require a prompt verbal apology in front of the entire class before the student leaves the conflict area.
Support regulation first, then hold a private process to review impact, choose a repair, and rehearse next steps.
Skip all restorative follow-up because discussing interpersonal impact feels stressful to a distressed learner.
Invite classmates to vote together on an appropriate classroom consequence and exact apology wording.
items.rationale: Restorative practice is most useful when the student can participate safely and with agency. A specific, private repair plus rehearsal teaches responsibility without forced disclosure, humiliation, or a purely punitive response.
choiceRationales: Forcing a public apology during active dysregulation risks humiliation and secondary escalation rather than genuine reflection or skill learning.

Correct. Restorative practice is most useful when the student can participate safely and with agency. A specific, private repair plus rehearsal teaches responsibility without forced disclosure, humiliation, or a purely punitive response.
Skipping follow-up altogether misses an opportunity—once the student is calm—to repair relationships and rehearse a better future response.
Having classmates vote on disciplinary punishments compromises student confidentiality, personal dignity, and trauma-aware restorative classroom boundaries.

items.prompt: A student will self-monitor sustained engagement during independent work. What should the teacher establish before using a timer and checklist?
choices: Use a broad verbal reminder to behave well and accept every self-recorded tally mark without verification.
Display the student’s self-monitoring tally chart publicly on the wall so classmates can double-check marks.
Define on-task behavior observably, teach the recording routine, and periodically check agreement directly.
Track final assignment grades in place of accuracy checks because self-monitoring needs no direct validation.
items.rationale: An observable definition and explicit practice make self-recording teachable. Occasional comparison with direct observation checks accuracy while preserving the student ownership that can support independence.
choiceRationales: Vague expectations like behaving well give the student no observable criterion to judge, making self-recorded marks inconsistent and uninformative.
Posting individual behavior charts publicly breaches confidentiality and creates peer stigma rather than supportive private self-regulation.

Correct. An observable definition and explicit practice make self-recording teachable. Occasional comparison with direct observation checks accuracy while preserving the student ownership that can support independence.
Grades alone do not confirm whether the student accurately recognizes and records on-task behavior during work intervals.

items.prompt: A student can list coping strategies but does not select one when initial tension appears. Which instruction is most likely to improve use?
choices: Wait for a peak crisis episode and introduce several brand-new coping options while tension is highest.
Assign one standard calming routine for every school setting without asking for the student’s preferences.
Reinforce reciting emotion vocabulary on flashcards without rehearsing an actionable coping response.
Teach individualized early cues, rehearse strategy choice while calm, prompt early, and monitor outcomes.
items.rationale: Strategy knowledge alone does not ensure timely use. Teaching antecedent cues, choice, calm rehearsal, and supported application builds fluency before high-intensity moments and provides evidence about which response works.
choiceRationales: Introducing unfamiliar coping steps during acute crisis overloads a dysregulated learner and prevents effective skill acquisition.
Imposing one rigid strategy across all contexts without student input lowers buy-in and may fit poorly in certain classrooms or peer settings.
Naming emotions without practicing concrete early-cue action steps does not bridge the gap between knowing a strategy and using it in real time.

Correct. Strategy knowledge alone does not ensure timely use. Teaching antecedent cues, choice, calm rehearsal, and supported application builds fluency before high-intensity moments and provides evidence about which response works.

items.prompt: A student needs repeated adult directions to complete the arrival routine. Which task-analysis approach best builds independence?
choices: Break the routine into observable steps, prompt only missed steps, reinforce completion, and fade systematically.
Deliver step-by-step adult verbal prompts every morning indefinitely so arrival errors stay rare.
Introduce every complex organization routine simultaneously without assessing which steps are already solid.
Complete any skipped morning organization steps quietly for the student without recording adult support.
items.rationale: A task analysis locates the exact teaching points and permits planned prompting and fading. Step-level data distinguish skill acquisition from adult completion and guide movement toward independent routine use.
choiceRationales: Correct. A task analysis locates the exact teaching points and permits planned prompting and fading. Step-level data distinguish skill acquisition from adult completion and guide movement toward independent routine use.
Continuous verbal directing keeps stimulus control on the adult and prevents the student from initiating arrival steps independently.
Teaching all steps without baseline assessment wastes time on mastered parts and overwhelms the student at genuine breakdown points.
Quietly finishing steps for the student masks support needs in the data and reinforces prompt dependence instead of independence.

items.prompt: A student wants to reduce call-outs during discussion. Which goal-setting routine most supports agency?
choices: Post the student’s daily call-out graph beside the classroom door to strengthen public accountability.
Co-create a realistic target, graph private data, review patterns together, and choose the next adjustment.
Select the behavioral criterion privately as staff and reveal progress only when report cards go home.
Record informal daily ratings of teacher frustration instead of counting observable hand-raising or call-outs.
items.rationale: Collaborative, private goal review makes the observable data useful to the learner and supports self-determination. Frequent reflection permits realistic adjustment without public shaming or reliance on subjective impressions.
choiceRationales: Posting individual behavior graphs publicly compromises student privacy and dignity and can trigger embarrassment or oppositional classroom escalation.

Correct. Collaborative, private goal review makes the observable data useful to the learner and supports self-determination. Frequent reflection permits realistic adjustment without public shaming or reliance on subjective impressions.
Setting goals without student input and delaying feedback until grading time removes learner agency and timely self-correction.
Measuring adult frustration reflects subjective impressions rather than objective student response counts needed for fair goal evaluation.

items.prompt: A school is considering check-in/check-out for a student with inconsistent morning engagement. What should determine whether it is appropriate?
choices: Enroll the student in check-in/check-out because every learner with EBD should participate in Tier 2 routines.
Launch the daily check-in sheet without defining measurable targets and keep it running through spring.
Align the routine to documented needs and likely reinforcers, gather student input, and track outcomes and fidelity.
Discontinue existing individualized IEP supports once the standard Tier 2 check-in routine begins.
items.rationale: A standardized support is not automatically functionally relevant. Individualized matching, voice, measurable outcomes, and fidelity checks allow the team to determine benefit and revise rather than treating placement in the intervention as the goal.
choiceRationales: Assigning check-in/check-out by eligibility label ignores whether adult attention is actually reinforcing or aversive for that specific learner.
Running an intervention all year without clear goals or data review wastes time and fails to detect whether the support is working.

Correct. A standardized support is not automatically functionally relevant. Individualized matching, voice, measurable outcomes, and fidelity checks allow the team to determine benefit and revise rather than treating placement in the intervention as the goal.

items.prompt: A learner acts impulsively during peer disagreement. Which strategy lesson is most likely to transfer?
